title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: The Battle of Borodino, followed by the occupation of Moscow and the flight of the French without further conflicts, is one of the most instructive phenomena in history.

All historians agree that the external activity of states and nations in their conflicts with one another is expressed through wars, and that military success or failure directly causes the political strength of states and nations to rise or fall.

It seems strange: some king or emperor quarrels with another, raises an army, fights the enemy's forces, wins by killing three, five, or ten thousand men, and thereby subjugates a kingdom and an entire nation of several million people. Yet as far as we know, every fact of history confirms the rule that the greater or lesser success of one army against another is the cause, or at least an essential indication, of a nation's strength rising or falling. This holds even though it is unintelligible that the defeat of an army—a hundredth part of a nation—should force the whole nation to submit. A victorious army wins, and at once the rights of the conquering nation grow at the expense of the defeated. A defeated army loses, and at once its people lose rights in proportion to the severity of the loss; if its army suffers a complete defeat, the nation is fully subjugated.

According to history, this has been true since the most ancient times, right up to the present day. All of Napoleon's wars confirm this rule. As Austria's army is defeated, Austria loses its rights, and France's rights and power grow. The French victories at Jena and Auerstadt destroy the independent existence of Prussia.

But then, in 1812, the French win a victory near Moscow. Moscow is taken, and after that—with no further battles—it isn't Russia that ceases to exist, but the French army of six hundred thousand, and then Napoleonic France itself. To bend the facts to fit the rules of history and say that the battlefield at Borodino remained in Russian hands, or that subsequent battles destroyed Napoleon's army, is impossible.

After the French victory at Borodino, there was no major engagement—nor any truly serious fighting—yet the French army ceased to exist. What does this mean? Suppose this had happened in the history of China: we might wave it off as 'not a historical phenomenon' (the historians' usual expedient when something doesn't fit their standards). Or suppose it had been only a brief skirmish with a handful of troops: we could call it an exception. But this happened before our fathers' eyes. For them it was a question of the life or death of their fatherland. And it took place in the greatest of all known wars.

The 1812 campaign, from the Battle of Borodino to the expulsion of the French, proved that winning a battle does not produce a conquest, and isn't even an invariable indicator of one. It proved that the force deciding the fate of nations lies not in conquerors, nor even in armies and battles, but in something else.

French historians, describing the state of the French army before it left Moscow, assert that everything was in order in the Grand Army except the cavalry, the artillery, and the transport—there was no forage for the horses or cattle. That was a misfortune no one could fix, since the peasants of the district burned their hay rather than let the French have it.

The victory that was won brought none of the usual results, because two peasants, Karp and Vlas—who after the French evacuated Moscow drove their carts in to loot the city, and who in general personally displayed no heroic feelings—along with the innumerable multitude of similar peasants, did not bring their hay to Moscow for the high prices offered them. They burned it instead.

Let's imagine two men fighting a duel with rapiers, following all the rules of fencing. The match has been going on for some time when one of them, feeling himself wounded and realizing this is no joke but a matter of life and death, throws down his rapier, grabs the first cudgel he can find, and starts swinging it. Now imagine that the combatant who so sensibly chose the simplest and best means to his end was also influenced by traditions of chivalry and, wishing to conceal what actually happened, insisted he had won his victory with the rapier according to all the rules of art. Imagine the confusion and obscurity that would result from such an account of the duel.

The fencer who demanded a contest according to the rules was the French army. His opponent, who threw away the rapier and grabbed the cudgel, was the Russian people. Those who try to explain the matter according to the rules of fencing are the historians who have described the event.

After the burning of Smolensk, a war began that followed no previous traditions. The burning of towns and villages, the retreats after battles, the blow struck at Borodino and the renewed retreat, the burning of Moscow, the capture of marauders, the seizure of supply trains, and guerrilla warfare—all were departures from the rules.

Napoleon felt this. From the time he assumed the correct fencing stance in Moscow and, instead of his opponent's rapier, saw a cudgel raised above his head, he never stopped complaining to Kutuzov and to Emperor Alexander that the war was being fought contrary to all the rules—as if there were any rules for killing people. The French complained that it wasn't fair play. Some highly placed Russians felt it was rather disgraceful to fight with a cudgel; they wanted to assume the fencing positions—en quarte or en tierce, according to all the rules—and deliver an adroit thrust en prime. But despite all of that, the cudgel of the people's war was raised with all its threatening, majestic strength and, without consulting anyone's preferences or rules and regardless of anything else, it rose and fell with stupid simplicity, but consistently, hammering the French until the entire invasion had perished.

And it is well for a people who do not—as the French did in 1813—salute according to all the rules of art, gracefully present the hilt of their rapier, and politely hand it to their magnanimous conqueror. It is well for a people who, at the moment of trial, without asking what rules others have followed in similar cases, simply and easily pick up the first cudgel at hand and strike with it until the feelings of resentment and revenge in their souls give way to contempt and compassion.
